title: Silent movie work and Satchel McVea
summary: He played atmosphere music on silent film sets, and Redd and Blakeney talk about Satchel McVea, who refused to join the union and found them work.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Back in L.A., still with Johnny Mitchell's band, we started playing theaters, clubs, dance halls, up and down the coast, including movies; the silent pictures, I'm talking about.
Mr. Blakeney, tell us a little bit about the movies and the conditions at that time for black musicians, mainly in the silent movies at that time.
We did quite a bit of work in silent movies, and one of the social hour jobs out there was Satchel McVea. (spelling).
Indeed a legend, Mr. Satchel McVea.

I was on one job out there with him, the name of the picture was Breakfast at Sunrise, at Universal, and the star was Constance Talmadge. In those days musicians would actually play to entertain the stars while they were acting.
That was during the
Yes. It was supposed to give them inspiration. If they wanted a sweet waltz we'd play that; if they wanted something hot we'd play that.
That was all atmospheric?
That's what it was, atmospheric.

Well you know Mr. Satchel McVea was indeed a legend. He was the father of Jack McVea and he started many musicians in Los Angeles playing; he played for many of the social affairs of the white community at that time. He was the father of Jack McVea and he was one of the black musicians that refused to join the union. He had quite a bit of work at that time without being a member of the musicians union, so he sort of rebelled and I don't think during his whole career he was ever a member of either Local 767 which was the
"colored union," or later Local 47. [He was] quite an important man in early musical history of Los Angeles.

That's right, he had plenty work and if myself or Ash Hardy, didn't have a steady job, we'd call him up and he'd say, 'Oh, yes, you're not working this Saturday, okay I got a job for you. How about next Wednesday, are you doing anything?' I can remember that; we'd call him our ace in the hole.
Satchel McVea. I never knew his given name.
Isaac.
He was a banjo player, he lived on East 34th Street in Los Angeles. What else can you tell us about the moving picture?
It's pretty hard to remember exactly, because we did so many in those days and there were so many one day affairs. You did the work for that day and
then you'd wait for the next call or something like that.

I remember playing a picture called the Night Nurse, I think it was Colleen Moore; it's pretty hard to remember because we played of them, in fact I worked in more silent pictures than I worked in talking pictures.
Maybe a little later on in our interview we will touch on the talking movies.
All I can remember about the silent movies, one picture--I forgot the name of it now--I remember that because we had it the whole week.
